library(dplyr)
library(gapminder)

Exercise 1 – Vectors, math & functions (Assignment 1 style). Create an object called temperature with the value 98.6. Then: Print temperature. Calculate the square root of temperature * 2. Test whether temperature is greater than 100. Check the class of temperature.

Temp <- 98.6
Temp2 <- sqrt(Temp*2)
Temp2
## [1] 14.04279
if(Temp>100){
  print("Temperature is above 100")
} else {
  print("Temperature is not above 100")
}
## [1] "Temperature is not above 100"
class(Temp)
## [1] "numeric"

Exercise 2 – dplyr filtering & arranging (Assignment 3 style)

Using the gapminder dataset:Filter rows where continent == “Europe” and year == 2007. Show at least 6 rows with head(…, 6). Arrange the result in descending order of lifeExp before displaying.

library(dplyr)
library(gapminder)   # needed — dplyr alone does not load the data

gapminder |>
  filter(continent == "Europe", year == 2007) |>
  arrange(desc(lifeExp)) |>
  head(6)

## 2 Switzerland Europe     2007    81.7  7554661    37506.
## 3 Spain       Europe     2007    80.9 40448191    28821.
## 4 Sweden      Europe     2007    80.9  9031088    33860.
## 5 France      Europe     2007    80.7 61083916    30470.

Exercise 3 – ggplot2 histogram + normality (Assignment 3 GGPLOT style)

Using the built-in trees dataset:

Create a histogram of Height with a different fill color (e.g., “steelblue”).

Run a Shapiro–Wilk test on Height and report the p-value.

State in a comment whether Height appears normally distributed (use α = 0.05).

library(ggplot2)
data("trees")

hist(trees$Height,
     main   = "Distribution of Height",
     xlab   = "Height (ft)",
     col    = "steelblue",
     border = "white")

sw <- shapiro.test(trees$Height)
sw
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  trees$Height
## W = 0.96545, p-value = 0.4034

Exercise 4 – Object manipulation & logicals. Create two objects x <- 12 and y <- 4. Then:

  • Calculate x divided by y and store it in z.
  • Print z.
  • Test whether z is equal to 3 (use ==).
  • Check the class of z.
x <- 12
y <- 4
z <- x / y
z
## [1] 3
z == 3
## [1] TRUE
class(z)
## [1] "numeric"

Exercise 5 – dplyr: select, filter, mutate (Assignment 3 style)

Using gapminder: - Keep only the columns country, year, and lifeExp. - Filter for country == "Cambodia". - Create a new column lifeExp_months = lifeExp * 12. - Show the first 6 rows of the result.

library(dplyr)
library(gapminder)
gapminder |>
  select(country, year, lifeExp) |>
  filter(country == "Cambodia") |>
  mutate(lifeExp_months = lifeExp * 12) |>
  head(6)
## # A tibble: 6 × 4
##   country   year lifeExp lifeExp_months

## 2 Cambodia  1957    41.4           496.
## 3 Cambodia  1962    43.4           521.
## 4 Cambodia  1967    45.4           545.
## 5 Cambodia  1972    40.3           484.
## 6 Cambodia  1977    31.2           375.

Exercise 6 – ggplot2 scatterplot + normality (Assignment 3 GGPLOT style)

Using the trees dataset: - Create a scatterplot of Volume (y-axis) vs Girth (x-axis), with color = "darkgreen". - Run a Shapiro–Wilk test on Volume. - In a comment, report the p-value and state whether Volume is normally distributed at α = 0.05.

library(ggplot2)
data("trees")
plot <- plot(
  trees$Girth ~ trees$Volume,
  type = "p",                      # line plot
  col = "darkgreen",                    # line color
  lwd = 2,                         # line width
  xlab = "Girth",  # x-axis label
  ylab = "Volume", # y-axis label
  main = "Relationship between Girth and Volume"
)

sw <- shapiro.test(trees$Volume)
sw
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  trees$Volume
## W = 0.88757, p-value = 0.003579
ggplot(trees, aes(x = Girth, y = Volume)) +
  geom_point(color = "darkgreen") +
  labs(title = "Relationship between Girth and Volume",
       x = "Girth", y = "Volume")

sw <- shapiro.test(trees$Volume)
sw            # W and p-value
## 
##  Shapiro-Wilk normality test
## 
## data:  trees$Volume
## W = 0.88757, p-value = 0.003579
sw$p.value    # explicit p-value
## [1] 0.003578866
# p-value < 0.05 → reject normality.
# Volume does NOT appear normally distributed at α = 0.05.

Exercise 7 – Grouped summary (Assignment 3 style) Using gapminder: Filter for year == 2007. Group by continent. Summarise the mean lifeExp (call it mean_lifeExp) and the mean gdpPercap (call it mean_gdp). Show the result (all rows are fine here — only 5 continents).

library(gapminder)
gapminder |>
  filter( year == "2007") |>
  group_by(continent) |>
  summarise(
    mean_lifeExp = mean(lifeExp),
    mean_gdp     = mean(gdpPercap)
  )
## # A tibble: 5 × 3
##   continent mean_lifeExp mean_gdp
##   <fct>            <dbl>    <dbl>
## 1 Africa            54.8    3089.
## 2 Americas          73.6   11003.
## 3 Asia              70.7   12473.
## 4 Europe            77.6   25054.
## 5 Oceania           80.7   29810.

Exercise 9 – ggplot2 boxplot + interpretation (Assignment 3 GGPLOT style)

Using gapminder: Filter for year == 2007. Create a boxplot of lifeExp grouped by continent (x = continent, y = lifeExp), filled with “tomato”. Rotate the x-axis labels 45° so they’re readable (hint: theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))). In a comment, state which continent has the highest median life expectancy based on the plot.

library(gapminder)


gapminder |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = continent, y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "tomato") +
  labs(title = "Life Expectancy by Continent (2007)",
       x = "Continent",
       y = "Life Expectancy") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

Exercise 10 – Counting rows per group (Assignment 3 style)

Using gapminder: - Filter for year == 2007. - Group by continent. - Summarise the number of countries in each continent using n() (call it n_countries). - Show the result.

library(dplyr)
library(gapminder)

gapminder |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  group_by(continent) |>
  summarise(n_countries = n())
## # A tibble: 5 × 2
##   continent n_countries
##   <fct>           <int>
## 1 Africa             52
## 2 Americas           25
## 3 Asia               33
## 4 Europe             30
## 5 Oceania             2

Hint: n() only works inside summarise()/mutate() after a group_by(). It returns the row count per group.

Exercise 12 – Vector stats + a line plot (mixed)

Using the built-in trees dataset: - Create a numeric vector vols <- trees$Volume. - Compute the mean and median of vols; print both. - Compute the standard deviation with sd(vols); print it. - Then create a line plot of Volume over Height using ggplot (geom_line()), with color = "purple".

library(ggplot2)
data("trees")

# 1. Calculate the stats
vols <- trees$Volume
Vmean <- mean(vols)
Vmedian <- median(vols)
SDVol <- sd(vols)

# Print them
Vmean
## [1] 30.17097
Vmedian
## [1] 24.2
SDVol
## [1] 16.43785
# 2. The Line Plot (Volume on Y, Height on X)
ggplot(trees, aes(x = Height, y = Volume)) +
  geom_line(color = "purple") +
  labs(title = "Volume over Height",
       x = "Height", y = "Volume")

Note: geom_line() connects points in the order they appear in the data, so for a meaningful line you’d normally sort by x first. For this exercise, just make the plot — no sorting required.

Exercise 13 – Base R stats & saving objects (Assignment 1 style). Using the built-in trees dataset: Create a vector girths <- trees$Girth. Calculate the variance of girths using var() and store it in an object called girth_var. Calculate the minimum and maximum of girths using min() and max(), and store them as girth_min and girth_max. Print all three objects (girth_var, girth_min, girth_max).

girths <- trees$Girth
girth_var <- var(girths)
girth_min <- min(girths)
girth_max <- max(girths)

girth_var
## [1] 9.847914
girth_max
## [1] 20.6
girth_min
## [1] 8.3

Exercise 14 – dplyr: filter, arrange, mutate, slice (Assignment 3 style)

Using gapminder: Filter for continent == “Asia” and year == 2007. Create a new column called pop_millions where population is divided by 1,000,000 (e.g., pop / 1000000). Arrange the result in descending order of pop_millions.

Keep only the top 5 rows and display them (use slice(1:5) or head(5)).

library(gapminder)

Exercise 15 – ggplot2 bar chart + interpretation (Assignment 3 GGPLOT style) Using gapminder: Filter for year == 2007. Use group_by() and summarise() to calculate the total population (sum(pop)) for each continent. Call the new column total_pop. Create a bar chart showing continent on the x-axis and total_pop on the y-axis. Fill the bars with “gold”. In a comment, state which continent has the largest total population in 2007.

Hint: In ggplot, use geom_col() to make a bar chart from pre-calculated values (like those from summarise()), whereas geom_bar() is used when you want ggplot to do the counting for you.

library(tidyverse)
## ── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
## ✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
## ✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
## ✔ purrr     1.2.2     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
## ✔ readr     2.2.0     
## ── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
## ✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
## ✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
## ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors
library(aod)

lizards |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Site, y = opalinus, fill = Site)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Distribution of opalinus counts under different light conditions",
       x = "Light condition",
       y = "Opalinus count")
